title: Redox Reactions: Electrons Trade Hands
hook: Rusting iron, burning wood, your body using oxygen to extract energy from food—all are redox reactions. Learn the electron trade.

slides.title: Redox Reactions
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao shows a copper coin turning green in air (oxidation) and asks: 'Why does metal tarnish? What's really happening at the atomic level?'

image.alt: Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidation & Reduction: A Tale of Electrons
slides.storyContext: Every redox reaction is an electron transfer. One atom LOSES electrons (oxidation), another GAINS (reduction). The atom losing electrons is the reducing agent; the one gaining is the oxidizing agent. Remember: 'OIL RIG' = Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

image.alt: Oxidation & Reduction: A Tale of Electrons — Redox Reactions

slides.title: The Electron Transfer Dance
slides.storyContext: Priya watches a demo: Dr. Rao dips a copper wire into silver nitrate solution. The wire becomes coated with shiny silver metal, while the solution turns blue. 'The copper atoms are giving up electrons to silver ions,' Dr. Rao explains. 'This is redox in real time. The electrons flow from copper to silver like water flowing downhill.'

points.text: Electrons flow from the atom being oxidized to the atom being reduced
The flow happens simultaneously—reduction cannot occur without oxidation
This is why we call it 'redox'—both processes are coupled

slides.inSimpleWords: Think of redox like a relay race: one atom hands off electrons (oxidation), the other receives them (reduction). Both happen at the same time.

image.alt: The Electron Transfer Dance — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidation States: Tracking Electrons

points.label: Definition
points.text: Number assigned to an atom reflecting electrons gained/lost. Range: -8 to +8 typically.

points.label: Rules (priority order)
points.text: 1. Element = 0. 2. Monatomic ion = charge. 3. O = -2 (except O₂²⁻ = -1, OF₂ O = +2). 4. H = +1 (except metal hydrides H = -1). 5. Halogens in compounds = -1. 6. Sum of all oxidation states = charge of compound.

example.problem: Find oxidation states in H₂SO₄.
example.solution: H = +1 (rule 4). O = -2 (rule 3). S = ? Sum: 2(+1) + S + 4(-2) = 0 → 2 + S - 8 = 0 → S = +6. (Sulfur in +6 state, even though it has only 6 valence e⁻—it's highly oxidized.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Oxidation states are electron-counting shortcuts. They tell you which atom lost electrons (oxidation state increases) and which gained (oxidation state decreases).

image.alt: Oxidation States: Tracking Electrons — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding Oxidation States
slides.storyContext: Arjun is struggling with oxidation states in complex ions. Dr. Rao walks him through step by step: for each ion, apply the rules in order and let the algebra solve for the unknown atom.

example.problem: Find oxidation states in the dichromate ion Cr₂O₇²⁻.
example.solution: O = -2 (rule 3), so 7 O atoms = -14. The ion has a -2 charge. Sum: 2(Cr) + 7(-2) = -2 → 2(Cr) - 14 = -2 → 2(Cr) = 12 → Cr = +6. Each chromium is in the +6 oxidation state (very oxidizing power).

slides.inSimpleWords: To find unknown oxidation states, use the rules as anchors, then use algebra to find the missing number.

slides.title: Identifying Redox Reactions

points.label: Redox?
points.text: Check if any atom's oxidation state CHANGES. If yes → redox.

points.label: Redox type (3 common)
points.text: (1) Combination (synthesis): A + B → AB. (2) Decomposition: AB → A + B. (3) Displacement: AB + C → AC + B.

points.label: Non-redox
points.text: Acid-base (H⁺ transfer), precipitation (ionic rearrangement). Oxidation states don't change.

example.problem: Is this redox? 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
example.solution: Mg: 0 → +2 (oxidation, lost 2 e⁻). O: 0 → -2 (reduction, gained 2 e⁻). YES, this is redox.

slides.inSimpleWords: If oxidation states change, it's a redox reaction. If they don't, it's something else (acid-base, precipitation).

image.alt: Identifying Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Recognizing Non-Redox Reactions
slides.storyContext: Priya mixes two solutions and watches a white precipitate form immediately. 'Is that redox?' Dr. Rao checks the oxidation states before and after. 'No change in oxidation states, so it's not redox. This is a precipitation reaction—ions rearranging, not transferring electrons.'

example.problem: Is AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) a redox reaction?
example.solution: Check oxidation states: Ag = +1 (before and after). Na = +1 (before and after). N = +5 (before and after). Cl = -1 (before and after). NO CHANGE. This is NOT redox—it's a precipitation reaction (ionic rearrangement).

slides.inSimpleWords: Not every reaction is redox. Acid-base neutralization and precipitation happen without electron transfer.

image.alt: Recognizing Non-Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Balancing Redox Equations: Half-Reaction Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Identify oxidation states. Which atom is oxidized? Which reduced?

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Write oxidation half-reaction (loses e⁻) and reduction half-reaction (gains e⁻).

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Balance atoms in each half-reaction (add H₂O, H⁺/OH⁻ as needed for acidic/basic solution).

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Balance electrons (multiply half-reactions so e⁻ gained = e⁻ lost).

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Add half-reactions. Cancel e⁻ and other species.

example.problem: Balance in acidic solution: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺
example.solution: Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Multiply first by 5: 5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻. Add: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O (balanced).

slides.inSimpleWords: Split the reaction into what's oxidized and what's reduced. Balance each half separately, then combine. This is the systematic way to handle complex redox.

image.alt: Balancing Redox Equations: Half-Reaction Method — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Worked Problem: Complex Redox Balancing
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao challenges the class with a reaction from industrial chemistry: dichromate oxidizing ethanol.

example.problem: Balance in acidic solution: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + C₂H₅OH → Cr³⁺ + C₂H₄O (acetaldehyde)
example.solution: C in ethanol: -2 → C in acetaldehyde: -1 (loses 1 e⁻ per C, 2 C total = 2 e⁻ lost). Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: +6 → Cr³⁺: +3 (gains 3 e⁻ per Cr, 2 Cr = 6 e⁻ gained). Multiply ethanol by 3: 3C₂H₅OH → 3C₂H₄O + 6e⁻. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6e⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Combined: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3C₂H₅OH + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3C₂H₄O + 7H₂O (balanced).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex redox balancing requires careful electron tracking. The half-reaction method handles it systematically—split, balance, multiply, combine.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Complex Redox Balancing — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Oxidizing & Reducing Agents

points.label: Oxidizing agent
points.text: Causes oxidation; itself gets reduced (gains electrons). Example: O₂ (oxygen is oxidizing everything else).

points.label: Reducing agent
points.text: Causes reduction; itself gets oxidized (loses electrons). Example: C (carbon reduces oxygen to CO₂).

points.label: Common agents
points.text: Strong oxidizers: F₂, Cl₂, H₂O₂, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇. Strong reducers: H₂, C, CO, metals like Zn, Fe.

example.problem: In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, identify the oxidizing and reducing agents.
example.solution: Na: 0 → +1 (oxidized). Cl₂: 0 → -1 (reduced). Na is the REDUCING agent (causes Cl to be reduced). Cl₂ is the OXIDIZING agent (causes Na to be oxidized).

slides.inSimpleWords: The reducing agent is oxidized (loses electrons); the oxidizing agent is reduced (gains electrons). The names describe what they DO, not what happens to them.

image.alt: Oxidizing & Reducing Agents — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Identifying Agents in Real Reactions
slides.storyContext: Arjun observes zinc reacting with dilute sulfuric acid, producing hydrogen gas. He needs to identify which species is oxidized and which is reduced, then name the agents.

example.problem: In Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂, identify the oxidizing and reducing agents.
example.solution: Zn: 0 → +2 (oxidized, loses 2e⁻). H: +1 → 0 (reduced, gains 1e⁻ per H, so 2e⁻ total). Zn is the REDUCING AGENT. H⁺ (in H₂SO₄) is the OXIDIZING AGENT.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look at oxidation state changes: the species that increases in oxidation state is oxidized (it's the reducing agent); the species that decreases is reduced (it's the oxidizing agent).

image.alt: Identifying Agents in Real Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Types of Redox Reactions

points.label: Combination (synthesis)
points.text: 2C + O₂ → 2CO. Both reactants change oxidation state.

points.label: Decomposition
points.text: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Single compound breaks; products have different oxidation states.

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. More reactive metal displaces less reactive from its salt.

points.label: Disproportionation
points.text: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO. Same element oxidized AND reduced in one reaction. Cl: 0 → -1 (in HCl, reduced) and 0 → +1 (in HClO, oxidized).

example.problem: Is Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O a disproportionation?
example.solution: Cl in Cl₂: 0. Cl in NaCl: -1 (reduced). Cl in NaClO: +1 (oxidized). YES, disproportionation. Same Cl atom family gains and loses electrons simultaneously.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox reactions come in patterns. Disproportionation is tricky—one atom is oxidized and reduced at the same time (like Cl in bleach production).

image.alt: Types of Redox Reactions — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Distinguishing Redox Types
slides.storyContext: Priya is given four reactions and must classify each as combination, decomposition, displacement, or disproportionation. She learns to recognize the patterns quickly.

points.label: Combination
points.text: Two simple substances or a simple + compound → one product (usually more complex)

points.label: Decomposition
points.text: One complex compound → two or more simpler products

points.label: Displacement
points.text: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from a compound

points.label: Disproportionation
points.text: Look for the same element at different oxidation states in products

example.problem: Classify: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
example.solution: Hydrogen: +1 (before and after). Oxygen: -1 (in H₂O₂) → -2 (in H₂O) and 0 (in O₂). Same element (oxygen) is both reduced and oxidized. This is DISPROPORTIONATION.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each redox type has a signature pattern. Learn to spot them, and you'll quickly classify any reaction.

image.alt: Distinguishing Redox Types — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Redox in Electrochemistry & Biology

points.label: Electrochemistry
points.text: Galvanic cells: redox reactions generate electrical current (battery). Electrolytic cells: electrical current drives redox reactions (electrolysis).

points.label: Respiration
points.text: Glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy. Glucose is oxidized (loses electrons); O₂ is reduced (gains electrons). Your body extracts energy this way.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: CO₂ + H₂O + light → glucose + O₂. Water is oxidized; CO₂ is reduced. Plants use sunlight to reverse respiration.

example.problem: In respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, identify which is oxidized and reduced.
example.solution: C in glucose: -2 to +4 (in CO₂). Oxidized. O in O₂: 0 → -2 (in H₂O & CO₂). Reduced. The electrons from C flow to O, releasing energy (~2800 kJ/mol)—this powers your cells.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox reactions power the world: electricity (galvanic cells), your body (respiration), and plants (photosynthesis). Electrons flowing = energy transfer.

image.alt: Redox in Electrochemistry & Biology — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Energy Transfer Through Redox: The Big Picture
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao connects redox chemistry to real life. 'Every time you eat, your cells perform redox to extract energy. Every time a battery powers your phone, redox reactions are running. Photosynthesis—also redox—stores solar energy in glucose. Redox is the engine of life and technology.'

example.problem: Explain how a Zn-Cu battery (galvanic cell) generates electricity using redox reactions.
example.solution: Zn electrode (anode): Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation, loses electrons). Cu electrode (cathode): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction, gains electrons). Electrons flow through an external circuit from Zn to Cu, creating electric current. The redox reaction IS the battery.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox doesn't just happen in test tubes—it powers every battery, every living cell, every solar panel.

image.alt: Energy Transfer Through Redox: The Big Picture — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Redox in Your Life: Rust & Corrosion
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees rust on a bicycle and asks: 'Why does iron rust, and how can we stop it?'

example.problem: Iron rusting: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → 4FeO·OH (rust). Identify oxidation states & the redox process.
example.solution: Fe: 0 → +3 (oxidized, loses 3e⁻ per Fe). O: 0 → -2 (reduced, gains 2e⁻ per O). This is a redox reaction. Prevention: paint (blocks O₂), galvanizing (coat with Zn, which oxidizes first), alloys (stainless steel, Cr prevents oxidation).

image.alt: Redox in Your Life: Rust & Corrosion — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Challenge: Analyze an Unknown Redox Reaction
slides.storyContext: Priya is given a mysterious reaction and must analyze it step by step: identify oxidation states, determine what's oxidized and reduced, name the agents, classify the type, and predict products.

example.problem: Balance and analyze: I₂ + Na₂S₂O₃ → NaI + Na₂S₄O₆ (thiosulfate reaction, used in photography)
example.solution: I in I₂: 0 → I in NaI: -1 (reduced). S in S₂O₃²⁻ has average +2 → S in S₄O₆²⁻ has average +2.5 (oxidized). I₂ is the oxidizing agent; S₂O₃²⁻ is the reducing agent. Balanced: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻. This is a redox reaction, and it's crucial in fixing photographic film.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use your redox skills to analyze any reaction: find oxidation states, track electron flow, name the agents, classify the type.

image.alt: Challenge: Analyze an Unknown Redox Reaction — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Challenge: Balancing in Basic Solution
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Dr. Rao about balancing redox reactions in basic solution instead of acidic. 'The method is similar, but we use OH⁻ instead of H⁺ and H₂O differently,' she explains.

example.problem: Balance in basic solution: MnO₄⁻ + Fe(OH)₂ → MnO₂ + Fe(OH)₃
example.solution: Mn: +7 → +4 (gains 3e⁻). Fe: +2 → +3 (loses 1e⁻). Oxidation: Fe(OH)₂ → Fe(OH)₃ + e⁻ (need to add OH⁻ to balance). Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 3e⁻ + 4H₂O → MnO₂ + 8OH⁻. Multiply oxidation by 3, add, and simplify. Final: MnO₄⁻ + 3Fe(OH)₂ + H₂O → MnO₂ + 3Fe(OH)₃.

slides.inSimpleWords: Balancing in basic solution uses the same half-reaction method, but with OH⁻ ions instead of H⁺.

image.alt: Challenge: Balancing in Basic Solution — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Step Redox Problem
slides.storyContext: Dr. Rao presents a challenging reaction sequence where Arjun must track electrons through multiple steps and balance a complex redox.

example.problem: In acidic solution, permanganate (MnO₄⁻) oxidizes oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻) to CO₂. Write and balance the half-reactions.
example.solution: Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (each C: +3 → +4). Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (Mn: +7 → +2). Multiply oxidation by 5, reduction by 2: 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ → 10CO₂ + 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex redox problems are solved by the half-reaction method: identify oxidation states, write half-reactions, balance electrons, combine.

image.alt: Challenge: Multi-Step Redox Problem — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Redox in Aqueous Solutions: Acidic vs. Basic

points.label: Acidic solution
points.text: Use H⁺ and H₂O to balance atoms after balancing electrons. Oxygen deficit? Add H₂O. Hydrogen excess? Add H⁺.

points.label: Basic solution
points.text: Convert by replacing H⁺ with OH⁻. For every H⁺, add an OH⁻ to both sides, then combine H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

points.label: Key difference
points.text: Acidic uses H⁺/H₂O; basic uses OH⁻/H₂O. The electron transfer is the same; only the medium changes.

example.problem: Convert the acidic solution redox equation to basic: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O
example.solution: Add 8OH⁻ to both sides: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ + 8OH⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O + 8OH⁻. Combine H⁺ + OH⁻ = H₂O: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 4H₂O → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 8OH⁻. This is the basic solution form.

slides.inSimpleWords: To convert redox from acidic to basic, replace H⁺ with OH⁻ equivalents and combine water molecules.

image.alt: Redox in Aqueous Solutions: Acidic vs. Basic — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Worked Example: Titration via Redox Reaction
slides.storyContext: Priya performs a permanganate titration to analyze the iron (II) content in a sample. This classic redox application teaches how stoichiometry and molarity work together in redox reactions.

example.problem: A 25.0 mL sample of Fe²⁺ solution is titrated with 0.02 M KMnO₄ solution. The endpoint occurs after 20 mL KMnO₄ is added. Find the molarity of Fe²⁺. (Balanced: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O)
example.solution: Moles of MnO₄⁻ = 0.02 M × 0.020 L = 0.0004 mol. From stoichiometry: 1 MnO₄⁻ : 5 Fe²⁺. Moles of Fe²⁺ = 5 × 0.0004 = 0.002 mol. Molarity of Fe²⁺ = 0.002 mol / 0.025 L = 0.08 M.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox titrations use stoichiometry from the balanced equation to determine unknown concentrations.

image.alt: Worked Example: Titration via Redox Reaction — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Challenge: Identify Unknown from Redox Behavior
slides.storyContext: Arjun is given an unknown metal and must identify it by observing how it reacts with an acid (redox displacement). Different metals oxidize at different rates and to different oxidation states.

example.problem: An unknown metal reacts with dilute HCl to produce H₂ gas and a +2 cation (MX₂ where X is Cl). Identify the metal.
example.solution: The metal is oxidized from 0 to +2, losing 2 electrons. H⁺ is reduced to H₂. Metals that form +2 cations with Cl: Fe, Zn, Cu, Ni, Mg, etc. The reaction rate and gas evolution speed can help narrow down (Mg reacts vigorously; Cu doesn't react with dilute HCl). Most likely: Zn or Fe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use redox reactions to identify unknown metals by observing their oxidation states and reaction rates.

image.alt: Challenge: Identify Unknown from Redox Behavior — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Real-World Redox: Batteries & Fuel Cells
slides.storyContext: Priya researches how redox reactions power the world. 'Every AA battery, every electric car, every space probe relies on redox chemistry inside. Fuel cells even use hydrogen (redox) to generate electricity without pollution.'

points.label: Battery chemistry
points.text: Zn–Cu galvanic cells, Pb–acid batteries in cars, Li-ion batteries in phones—all use redox to generate voltage.

points.label: Fuel cells
points.text: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (redox) generates electricity directly, with water as the only exhaust.

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox reactions aren't just lab chemistry—they power your devices, vehicles, and homes.

image.alt: Real-World Redox: Batteries & Fuel Cells — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Electron-Transfer Series & Reactivity

points.label: Activity series
points.text: Metals ranked by tendency to lose electrons (be oxidized). More active metals oxidize more easily.

points.label: Reactivity order (decreasing)
points.text: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au. A metal higher in the series can displace a lower one from a salt.

points.label: Predicting reactions
points.text: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (Fe is more reactive, displaces Cu). Cu + FeSO₄ → No reaction (Cu is less reactive).

example.problem: Predict: (1) Zn + CuCl₂ → ? (2) Ag + ZnCl₂ → ?
example.solution: (1) Zn is more active than Cu (Zn higher in series). Zn + CuCl₂ → ZnCl₂ + Cu (reaction occurs). (2) Ag is less active than Zn. No reaction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the activity series to predict whether a metal will displace another from a solution.

image.alt: Electron-Transfer Series & Reactivity — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Challenge: Real-World Redox Corrosion Control
slides.storyContext: Arjun investigates how to protect iron from rust using redox chemistry. 'Can I use another metal to protect it?' Dr. Rao smiles. 'Yes—use a metal above iron in the activity series, called sacrificial protection.'

example.problem: Zinc-coated (galvanized) steel is more rust-resistant than bare steel. Explain using redox and the activity series.
example.solution: Zn is above Fe in the activity series. Zn is oxidized first (2Zn → 2Zn²⁺ + 4e⁻), protecting Fe from oxidation. Even if the Zn coating scratches, Zn continues to protect Fe electrochemically (sacrificial anode). Only after Zn is depleted does Fe oxidize and rust.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the activity series to protect metals: coat with a more reactive metal (sacrificial anode) that oxidizes first.

image.alt: Challenge: Real-World Redox Corrosion Control — Redox Reactions

slides.title: Redox Reactions Summary

points.text: Oxidation = loss of electrons (oxidation state increases)
Reduction = gain of electrons (oxidation state decreases)
Redox reactions involve electron transfer between atoms
Oxidation states track electrons; sum to compound charge
Half-reaction method: split into oxidation & reduction, balance, multiply, combine
Oxidizing agent is reduced; reducing agent is oxidized
Redox powers batteries, respiration, and industry

slides.inSimpleWords: Redox is electron transfer. Atoms that lose electrons are oxidized; those that gain are reduced. Mastering redox balancing (half-reaction method) is key to Class 11 chemistry.

title: Rajesh's Organic Chemistry Lab: Building Blocks of Life
hook: Follow Rajesh as he discovers why carbon creates millions of compounds and learns to detect, separate, and identify them.

characters.name: Rajesh
characters.role: Class 11 chemistry student exploring organic compounds

slides.title: Organic Chemistry: Building Blocks of Life
slides.storyContext: Rajesh walks into Dr. Sharma's lab one afternoon and sees bottles of unknown liquids. 'These are all organic compounds,' Dr. Sharma explains. 'Every living thing—the food you eat, the clothes you wear, the paper in your notebook—is made of them. Today, you'll learn how they're built and how to identify them.'

image.alt: Organic Chemistry: Building Blocks of Life — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: The Story Begins: Why Carbon Is Special
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma holds up a piece of coal and a diamond. 'Both are pure carbon, yet one is soft and black, the other hard and clear. Carbon's magic is that it forms millions of compounds—more than all other elements combined. Why? Because it has 4 valence electrons and can form 4 strong covalent bonds, often with other carbons, creating long chains and rings.'

points.text: Carbon forms 4 covalent bonds (tetravalency)
Bonds can be C–C, C–H, C–O, C–N, etc.
Carbon chains and rings create structural diversity

slides.inSimpleWords: Carbon is the champion bonder—it can connect to 4 other atoms at once, and often connects to itself, making huge chains and patterns.

image.alt: The Story Begins: Why Carbon Is Special — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Carbon's Versatility: Chains, Rings, and Bonds
slides.storyContext: Priya draws different structures on the whiteboard. 'Look—all these have the same molecular formula C₆H₁₂, but different structures: a straight chain, a branched chain, a ring. Carbon's ability to bond with itself in so many ways explains why there are millions of organic compounds.' Dr. Sharma nods. 'And that's just considering structure. Wait until we learn about functional groups.'

points.label: Linear chains
points.text: Carbons in a line: butane is CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃

points.label: Branched chains
points.text: Side groups attached: isobutane is (CH₃)₃CH

points.label: Rings (cyclic)
points.text: Carbons forming closed loops: cyclohexane is a 6-membered ring

slides.inSimpleWords: Carbon can twist, branch, and loop—creating an endless variety of shapes with the same atoms.

image.alt: Carbon's Versatility: Chains, Rings, and Bonds — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Homologous Series: Cousins in Chemistry
slides.storyContext: Priya opens a kitchen cabinet in her house. 'Look, Dr. Sharma—butter (animal fat), cooking oil (vegetable), and kerosene (for lamps). They all feel oily, but they're different!' Dr. Sharma nods. 'That's a homologous series. Each differs by a CH₂ unit, follows the same general formula, and has similar chemical properties.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A series of compounds differing by successive CH₂ (methylene) units

points.label: General formula
points.text: All alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; all alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ; all alcohols: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O

points.label: Trend
points.text: As the chain grows: boiling point increases, density increases, reactivity decreases

points.label: Examples
points.text: CH₄ (methane), C₂H₆ (ethane), C₃H₈ (propane)—each differ by CH₂

example.problem: Ethane is C₂H₆, bp = −88.5°C. Propane is C₃H₈, bp = −42.1°C. Which is more volatile?
example.solution: Ethane. Its lower molar mass and weaker intermolecular forces mean it boils at a much lower temperature, so it evaporates faster.

slides.inSimpleWords: A homologous series is like a family of compounds. Each one is the previous one plus a CH₂ piece, so they're related but not identical.

image.alt: Homologous Series: Cousins in Chemistry — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Predicting Properties in a Homologous Series
slides.storyContext: Rajesh plots a graph of boiling points vs. molecular weight for the alkane family (methane through decane). 'There's a pattern!' Dr. Sharma confirms: 'As you add CH₂, you add about 30 g/mol and the boiling point increases by roughly 20°C per CH₂. Homologous series are predictable.'

example.problem: Methane (CH₄) has bp = −161°C. Predict the boiling point of ethane (C₂H₆) using the trend.
example.solution: Methane → Ethane is one CH₂ addition. Rough increase ≈ +20°C per CH₂. Predicted bp ≈ −161 + 20 = −141°C. Actual bp = −88.5°C (the trend is rough for very small molecules, but improves for larger ones). The principle holds: larger homologs boil at higher temperatures.

slides.inSimpleWords: In a homologous series, properties change predictably as you add CH₂ units.

image.alt: Predicting Properties in a Homologous Series — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Isomerism: Same Atoms, Different Shapes
slides.storyContext: Rajesh arranges colored beads on a string. 'I can make the same beads into different patterns—a line or a loop!' Dr. Sharma smiles. 'Exactly. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements. The atoms rearrange, and the properties change. Let's explore two main types.'

points.label: Structural isomerism
points.text: Atoms bonded in different orders (chain isomers, position isomers, functional group isomers)

points.label: Example: C₄H₁₀
points.text: Butane (straight chain) vs. isobutane (branched)—same formula, different bp and properties

points.label: Stereoisomerism
points.text: Same structure, but atoms arranged differently in space (cis/trans, optical)

example.problem: C₃H₈O can be 1-propanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) or 2-propanol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃). Are they isomers?
example.solution: Yes. Both have 3 carbons, 8 hydrogens, 1 oxygen. But they're position isomers—the OH group attaches at different positions, so they have different chemical properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Isomers are like anagrams in chemistry—same letters (atoms) rearranged into different words (structures).

image.alt: Isomerism: Same Atoms, Different Shapes — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding All Isomers
slides.storyContext: Priya is asked to draw all structural isomers of C₄H₁₀. She systematically organizes them: 4-carbon chain, 3-carbon chain with a methyl branch.

points.label: n-Butane
points.text: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (straight 4-carbon chain, bp = −0.5°C)

points.label: Isobutane (2-methylpropane)
points.text: (CH₃)₃CH or CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ (3-carbon chain with methyl branch, bp = −11.7°C)

points.label: No other isomers
points.text: These two are the only C₄H₁₀ isomers (only two ways to connect 4 carbons with single bonds)

example.problem: How many structural isomers does C₅H₁₂ have?
example.solution: Three: (1) n-pentane (straight 5-carbon chain), (2) isopentane (4-carbon chain with methyl branch at C2), (3) neopentane (3-carbon chain with two methyl branches at C2). All have the same formula C₅H₁₂, but different structures and boiling points.

slides.inSimpleWords: Isomers are real compounds with the same formula but different structures. More carbons = more possible isomers.

image.alt: Worked Example: Finding All Isomers — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: IUPAC Nomenclature: Naming the Compounds
slides.storyContext: Rajesh looks at a bottle labeled 'CH₃CH₂CH₂OH' and then another labeled 'propan-1-ol'. 'They're the same, but one is systematic!' Dr. Sharma explains IUPAC rules: identify the longest carbon chain (main functional group determines name), number from the end nearest the functional group, then list substituents alphabetically.

points.label: Parent chain
points.text: 1=methane, 2=ethane, 3=propane, 4=butane, 5=pentane, etc.

points.label: Functional group suffix
points.text: –ane (alkane), –ene (alkene), –yne (alkyne), –ol (alcohol), –al (aldehyde)

points.label: Numbering
points.text: Start from the end closest to the main functional group

points.label: Example
points.text: CH₃–CHBr–CH₂–CH₃ is 2-bromobutane (4 carbons, Br at position 2)

example.problem: Name the compound: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–OH
example.solution: Longest chain = 3 carbons, alcohol (OH) → main is 'propan-1-ol' or 'propanol'. But a methyl branch at C2 → 2-methylpropan-1-ol (or isobutanol).

slides.inSimpleWords: IUPAC names are like addresses: identify the main street (longest carbon chain), the house (functional group), and say where the mailbox (substituent) is.

image.alt: IUPAC Nomenclature: Naming the Compounds — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Mastering IUPAC Naming
slides.storyContext: Priya practices naming increasingly complex organic compounds. Dr. Sharma gives tips: always find the longest chain first, then locate and number the main functional group, then name any branches.

example.problem: Name: CH₃–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃
example.solution: Longest chain = 6 carbons (hexane). Main group = OH at position 3 (number from nearest end: 3 is closer than 4). Branches = methyl at position 4. Name: 4-methylhexan-3-ol.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice finding the longest chain, numbering from the functional group, and adding substituent names alphabetically.

slides.title: Detection & Identification: Qualitative Analysis
slides.storyContext: Priya brings test tubes to the lab table. 'Rajesh, I'm given three unknowns: one with C, one with N, one with S. How do I detect what's inside?' Dr. Sharma explains the classic tests: burn a tiny sample in a copper oxide tube and test the products, use sodium fusion, then apply specific reagent tests.

points.label: Carbon (C)
points.text: Burn in CuO: black residue of C → lime water turns milky (CO₂ produced)

points.label: Hydrogen (H)
points.text: Combustion produces H₂O; use anhydrous CaCl₂ to absorb it (mass increase)

points.label: Nitrogen (N)
points.text: Sodium fusion: compound + Na → cyanide → add FeSO₄ + FeCl₃ → Prussian blue color (Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃)

points.label: Sulfur (S)
points.text: Sodium fusion + FeCl₃ → black precipitate of FeS

example.problem: An organic compound burns to give CO₂, H₂O, and a pungent gas. What elements are present?
example.solution: C (CO₂ is produced), H (H₂O is produced). The pungent gas is likely SO₂ (sulfur) or NO₂ (nitrogen). Run a sodium fusion test to confirm.

slides.inSimpleWords: To identify elements in an unknown compound, burn it carefully, collect the products, and run chemical tests on them—like a detective gathering clues.

image.alt: Detection & Identification: Qualitative Analysis — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Worked Example: Detecting Elements Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Rajesh performs qualitative analysis on an unknown compound. He follows the systematic procedure: combustion, then sodium fusion, then specific tests.

points.label: Step 1: Combustion test
points.text: Heat sample in CuO. Gas products are CO₂ (turns lime water milky) and H₂O (absorbed by CaCl₂). Elements confirmed: C and H.

points.label: Step 2: Sodium fusion
points.text: Fuse sample with Na metal. This breaks all bonds involving C, H, N, S and produces ionic products (cyanides, sulfides).

points.label: Step 3: Test for N
points.text: Add FeSO₄ + FeCl₃ to the fusion product. If Prussian blue forms, N is present.

points.label: Step 4: Test for S
points.text: Add dilute HCl to another portion. If black FeS forms (from FeCl₃ added), S is present.

example.problem: An unknown compound gives these results: (1) Combustion produces CO₂ and H₂O. (2) Sodium fusion + FeSO₄/FeCl₃ → blue color. (3) Black precipitate forms when HCl is added. What elements are present?
example.solution: C and H (from combustion). N (Prussian blue test confirms it). S (black precipitate confirms it). The unknown contains C, H, N, and S.

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow the systematic tests in order: combustion first, then sodium fusion, then specific reagent tests for N, S, and halogens.

image.alt: Worked Example: Detecting Elements Step by Step — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Quantitative Analysis: Measuring the Formula
slides.storyContext: Rajesh sets up a combustion apparatus. 'I'll measure exactly how much CO₂ and H₂O a sample produces, then work backward to find the empirical and molecular formulas.' This method, called combustion analysis, reveals the exact proportions of each element in the compound.

points.label: Empirical formula
points.text: The simplest whole-number ratio of elements (e.g., CH₂O)

points.label: Molecular formula
points.text: The actual formula (e.g., C₆H₁₂O₆ = glucose)

points.label: Combustion method
points.text: Burn sample in O₂, collect & weigh CO₂ and H₂O, calculate moles of C and H

points.label: Procedure step
points.text: Moles of C from CO₂; moles of H from H₂O; moles of O from sample mass minus C and H

example.problem: 0.2 g of a hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ yields 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O. Find the empirical formula.
example.solution: Moles of CO₂ = 0.44/44 = 0.01; moles of C = 0.01. Moles of H₂O = 0.18/18 = 0.01; moles of H = 0.02. Ratio C:H = 0.01:0.02 = 1:2 → empirical formula is CH₂.

slides.inSimpleWords: Burn an unknown compound completely, weigh what comes out, then use math to figure out what was inside.

image.alt: Quantitative Analysis: Measuring the Formula — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Worked Example: From Unknown to Identified
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma gives Rajesh and Priya a mystery bottle. Together they work through the full identification process—a real scientist's workflow.

points.label: Step 1: Qualitative
points.text: Burn sample → produces CO₂ and H₂O → contains C and H. Sodium fusion → Prussian blue → contains N.

points.label: Step 2: Quantitative
points.text: Combustion analysis: 0.15 g sample → 0.22 g CO₂, 0.18 g H₂O, 0.03 g N

points.label: Step 4: Ratio
points.text: C:H:N = 0.06:0.02:0.002 = 30:10:1. Empirical formula: C₃₀H₁₀N (or simplified to find MW)

example.problem: A 0.15 g sample of an organic compound gives 0.22 g CO₂, 0.18 g H₂O, and 0.03 g N₂ (from nitrogen). What is the empirical formula?
example.solution: Moles: C = 0.22/44 = 0.005 mol → mass 0.06 g; H = 0.18/18 = 0.01 mol → mass 0.01 g; N = 0.03/28 = 0.001 mol. Empirical mass ≈ 0.08 g. Ratio C:H:N ≈ 5:10:1 → empirical formula C₅H₁₀N (or verify with molecular weight).

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow the full detective workflow: identify what's there, measure exact amounts, do the math, find the formula.

image.alt: Worked Example: From Unknown to Identified — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Challenge: Identify the Mystery Compound
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and Priya are given a colorless liquid that smells slightly fruity. They perform combustion analysis and find: 0.1 g sample → 0.176 g CO₂ and 0.108 g H₂O. Assume it contains only C, H, and O. Can they determine the empirical formula?

example.problem: 0.1 g of an organic compound (C, H, O only) burns to give 0.176 g CO₂ and 0.108 g H₂O. What is the empirical formula?
example.solution: Moles of C = 0.176/44 = 0.004 mol; mass of C = 0.004 × 12 = 0.048 g. Moles of H = 0.108/18 = 0.006 mol; mass of H = 0.006 × 1 = 0.006 g. Mass of O = 0.1 − 0.048 − 0.006 = 0.046 g; moles of O = 0.046/16 ≈ 0.00288 mol. Ratio C:H:O ≈ 0.004:0.006:0.00288 = 1.4:2.1:1 ≈ 7:10.5:5 = 14:21:10 = 7:10.5:5. Simplify: approximately C₂H₃O. (A typical answer: C₂H₃O or C₂H₄O₂, depending on rounding.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use combustion data and mass calculations to reverse-engineer the empirical formula.

image.alt: Challenge: Identify the Mystery Compound — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Challenge: Name Complex Organic Structures
slides.storyContext: Priya is given several complex organic structures with multiple functional groups and branches. She must apply IUPAC nomenclature systematically to name each one correctly.

example.problem: Name: CH₃–CH(Br)–CH(OH)–CH₂–CHO (aldehyde with alcohol and bromine)
example.solution: Main functional group: aldehyde (CHO) at C5. Longest chain = 5 carbons (pentanal). OH at C3, Br at C2. Number from aldehyde end: 1 = CHO, 2 = Br, 3 = OH. Branches are listed alphabetically (bromo before hydroxy). Name: 2-bromopentane-3-ol-1-al, or more commonly: 2-bromo-3-hydroxypentanal.

slides.inSimpleWords: For complex molecules with multiple functional groups, prioritize: identify the main functional group (highest priority), then name substituents.

image.alt: Challenge: Name Complex Organic Structures — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Functional Groups: The Key to Organic Reactivity

points.label: Definition
points.text: Specific groups of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical reactions. Same functional group = similar reactions.

points.label: Common groups
points.text: Alcohol (–OH), aldehyde (–CHO), ketone (C=O), carboxylic acid (–COOH), amine (–NH₂), ether (–O–), alkene (C=C)

points.label: Reactivity
points.text: The functional group, not the carbon chain, determines how a molecule reacts.

example.problem: Why does ethanol (C₂H₅OH) react with sodium but ethane (C₂H₆) doesn't?
example.solution: Ethanol has an –OH group (alcohol), which is reactive and donates hydrogen. The reaction: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. Ethane has no functional group, only C–C and C–H bonds (very stable, won't react with Na at room temperature).

slides.inSimpleWords: Functional groups are the reactive parts of organic molecules. Same functional group = similar chemistry, regardless of the carbon chain attached.

image.alt: Functional Groups: The Key to Organic Reactivity — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Worked Example: Classifying Organic Reactions
slides.storyContext: Priya is given several organic reactions and must classify them (substitution, addition, elimination) based on what happens to the functional group.

example.problem: Classify: (1) CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr (2) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH (3) CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
example.solution: (1) SUBSTITUTION: Br is replaced by OH. (2) ADDITION: H₂O adds across the double bond. (3) ELIMINATION: H₂O is removed from the alcohol, forming a double bond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Organic reactions are classified as substitution (swap), addition (add across a double bond), or elimination (remove a small molecule).

image.alt: Worked Example: Classifying Organic Reactions — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Challenge: Deduce Structure from Molecular Formula & Reactions
slides.storyContext: Rajesh is given a molecular formula (C₄H₁₀O), told it reacts with sodium (producing H₂), and asked to deduce the structure. He must use functional group clues.

example.problem: A compound with formula C₄H₁₀O reacts vigorously with Na to produce H₂ and a salt. What is the structure?
example.solution: The formula C₄H₁₀O suggests 1 degree of unsaturation (possibly 1 ring or 1 double bond, but the H count suggests a single functional group). Reaction with Na → produces H₂ → the compound is an ALCOHOL (–OH). Possible structures: 1-butanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH), 2-butanol, or isopropanol. The formula and reaction confirm one of these alcohol isomers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use molecular formula and known reactions to deduce structure—alcohol reacts with Na; alkene adds bromine; carboxylic acid turns blue litmus red.

image.alt: Challenge: Deduce Structure from Molecular Formula & Reactions — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Organic Chemistry in Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Priya reflects on where organic chemistry appears in daily life. 'The food I eat (carbohydrates, proteins, fats), the clothes I wear (cotton cellulose, synthetic polymers), the medicines I take—all are organic compounds. Every product in a pharmacy is built on carbon chemistry.'

points.text: Pharmaceuticals: aspirin, penicillin, vitamins—all synthesized from simple organic precursors
Materials: plastics, rubber, ceramics—based on organic polymers or carbon compounds
Food: glucose, amino acids, lipids—carbon-based molecules that sustain life

slides.inSimpleWords: Organic chemistry is everywhere—in your body, your food, your clothes, and your medicines.

slides.title: Separation & Purification Techniques

points.label: Distillation
points.text: Separates liquids based on boiling point. Useful for fractional distillation of crude oil or separating volatile solvents.

points.label: Chromatography
points.text: Separates mixtures based on differential adsorption. Paper chromatography separates dyes and pigments.

points.label: Crystallization
points.text: Isolates solids by dissolving in hot solvent, then cooling to precipitate pure crystals.

example.problem: How would you separate a mixture of ethanol (bp 78°C) and water (bp 100°C)?
example.solution: Use distillation: heat the mixture to 78–100°C. Ethanol, having the lower bp, evaporates first and is collected in the condenser. Water remains behind or is collected later at higher temperature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distillation, chromatography, and crystallization are laboratory tools for separating and purifying organic compounds.

image.alt: Separation & Purification Techniques — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Reaction Mechanisms: How Organic Reactions Work

points.label: Mechanism
points.text: Step-by-step description of how bonds break and form during a reaction.

points.label: SN1 vs SN2
points.text: SN2 (bimolecular): fast, direct displacement, inversion of stereochemistry. SN1 (unimolecular): slow, two-step, via carbocation, racemization.

points.label: Addition mechanism
points.text: Alkene's π electrons attack an electrophile; carbocation forms; nucleophile attacks.

example.problem: Draw the SN2 mechanism for: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻
example.solution: OH⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the carbon from behind the C–Br bond, pushing Br⁻ out in one concerted step. No intermediate. Stereochemistry inverts (Walden inversion).

slides.inSimpleWords: Reaction mechanisms show how electrons move to break and form bonds—the detailed choreography of organic reactions.

image.alt: Reaction Mechanisms: How Organic Reactions Work — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Green Chemistry: Sustainable Organic Synthesis
slides.storyContext: Priya learns about green chemistry: designing reactions that minimize waste, energy, and toxicity. 'Modern organic chemistry cares not just about making compounds, but doing it sustainably.'

example.problem: Why is water a preferred solvent in green organic chemistry compared to traditional organic solvents like benzene or chloroform?
example.solution: Water is renewable, nontoxic, nonflammable, and abundant. Reactions in water are often safer and produce less hazardous waste. Benzene and chloroform are toxic/carcinogenic and persist in the environment.

slides.inSimpleWords: Green chemistry applies organic principles to make safer, more sustainable products and processes.

image.alt: Green Chemistry: Sustainable Organic Synthesis — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Challenge: Multistep Synthesis Planning
slides.storyContext: Rajesh is challenged to design a synthesis route from ethane (C₂H₆) to ethanoic acid (acetic acid, CH₃COOH) using a sequence of organic reactions.

example.problem: Design a route: C₂H₆ → CH₃COOH
example.solution: Step 1: C₂H₆ + Br₂ (UV) → C₂H₅Br (free-radical substitution). Step 2: C₂H₅Br + KOH (alcoholic) → C₂H₄ (elimination). Step 3: C₂H₄ + H₂O (H₂SO₄) → C₂H₅OH (hydration/addition). Step 4: 2C₂H₅OH + O₂ (catalyst/oxidation, e.g., Cu) → 2CH₃CHO (oxidation to aldehyde). Step 5: CH₃CHO + [O] (further oxidation, e.g., KMnO₄) → CH₃COOH (acetic acid).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multistep synthesis requires planning a sequence of reactions, each building on the previous product.

image.alt: Challenge: Multistep Synthesis Planning — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Formula Determination from Combustion: Full Walkthrough
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma walks Rajesh through a complete problem: from combustion data to molecular formula (using molar mass).

example.problem: 0.2 g of an organic compound (C, H, O only) yields 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O. Molar mass = 120 g/mol. Find the molecular formula.
example.solution: Empirical formula (from combustion): moles of C = 0.44/44 = 0.01, moles of H = 0.18/18 × 2 = 0.02, moles of O = 0.2−(0.01×12)−(0.02×1) / 16 ≈ 0.00625 → C:H:O = 0.01:0.02:0.00625 = 8:16:5 = C₈H₁₆O₅. Empirical mass ≈ 240. Molecular mass ÷ empirical = 120/60 = 2 (approx). Molecular formula ≈ C₄H₈O₂ or close.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use combustion data + molar mass to determine both empirical and molecular formulas.

image.alt: Formula Determination from Combustion: Full Walkthrough — Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques

slides.title: Challenge: Complete Organic Analysis Problem
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma presents a final capstone problem combining qualitative tests, quantitative combustion analysis, and structure deduction.

example.problem: An organic liquid: (1) burns to CO₂ & H₂O only, (2) shows no color change with Br₂ water, (3) 0.1 g yields 0.165 g CO₂ and 0.09 g H₂O. What is the empirical formula?
example.solution: From combustion: C = 0.165/44 = 0.00375 mol (0.045 g); H = 0.09/18 × 2 = 0.01 mol (0.01 g); O = 0.1 − 0.045 − 0.01 = 0.045 g = 0.0028 mol. Ratio C:H:O = 0.00375:0.01:0.0028 = 1.3:3.6:1 ≈ 13:36:10 = 13:36:10. Close to C₂H₆O (methanol, ethanol) or C₃H₈O (propanol). No Br₂ color change → no C=C (alcohol, not alkene). Likely ethanol C₂H₅OH or similar.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine qualitative tests and quantitative combustion data to identify organic compounds completely.

slides.title: What Are Hydrocarbons? The Carbon–Hydrogen Bond
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma draws the simplest hydrocarbon: methane, CH₄. 'One carbon, four hydrogens. Carbon forms four C–H bonds. But carbon can also bond to other carbons, creating chains and rings. This is the foundation of all hydrocarbons and all organic molecules. The type and arrangement of these C–C bonds determine everything.'

points.text: Hydrocarbons contain only C and H
Can be classified by C–C bond type: single (–), double (=), or triple (≡)
Can be chain (open-ended) or cyclic (rings)
Most are nonpolar, hydrophobic, and found in crude oil and coal

slides.title: Hydrocarbons from the Earth
slides.storyContext: Neha researches the origins of hydrocarbons. 'Crude oil comes from ancient dead organisms. Coal is ancient vegetation. Ms. Verma nods. 'And we use hydrocarbons not just for fuel, but for plastics, medicines, textiles, and thousands of products.'

points.label: Natural sources
points.text: Crude oil: mixture of alkanes and other hydrocarbons; coal: aromatic and aliphatic compounds

points.label: Refining
points.text: Crude oil is separated by boiling point into fractions: LPG, petrol, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen

points.label: Uses beyond fuel
points.text: Plastics (polyethylene from ethene), medicines, dyes, solvents, lubricants

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons are fossil fuels—ancient organic matter converted into energy and materials over millions of years.

slides.title: Classification: Saturated vs. Unsaturated
slides.storyContext: Arun opens an old bottle of sesame oil and a bottle of vegetable oil from his kitchen. 'Ms. Verma, why does the sesame oil feel thicker and last longer?' Ms. Verma explains: saturated fats are like full trains—no more seats (C–C single bonds only). Unsaturated fats have gaps—they can still pick up passengers (double/triple bonds). This affects how tightly they pack and how they react.

points.label: Alkanes (Saturated)
points.text: Only C–C single bonds, formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Examples: CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈. Unreactive.

points.label: Alkenes (Unsaturated)
points.text: At least one C=C double bond, formula CₙH₂ₙ. Examples: C₂H₄ (ethene), C₃H₆ (propene). Reactive.

points.label: Alkynes (Unsaturated)
points.text: At least one C≡C triple bond, formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Examples: C₂H₂ (acetylene). Very reactive.

example.problem: Propane (C₃H₈) and propene (C₃H₆) have the same carbons but different formulas. Why, and how does that affect their properties?
example.solution: Propane has only C–C single bonds (saturated); propene has one C=C double bond (unsaturated). Propene is more reactive—it readily undergoes addition reactions (adding H₂, Br₂, etc.) because the double bond can break and form new bonds. Propane is inert unless heated or exposed to a catalyst.

slides.inSimpleWords: Saturated hydrocarbons are fully bonded and lazy; unsaturated ones have a double or triple bond, which makes them eager to react.

image.alt: Classification: Saturated vs. Unsaturated — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkanes: The Saturated Series
slides.storyContext: Neha researches hydrocarbon sources. 'Natural gas is mostly methane. Petrol is a mixture of alkanes. Coal is ancient alkanes and aromatics.' Ms. Verma nods. 'Alkanes are the most stable hydrocarbons. They're found in crude oil, and we refine them for energy. Let's look at their properties and reactions.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for acyclic alkanes; CₙH₂ₙ for cycloalkanes

points.label: Bonding
points.text: All C–C and C–H bonds are sigma (σ) bonds; no π bonds

points.label: Properties
points.text: Nonpolar, hydrophobic, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, low reactivity

points.label: Main reactions
points.text: Combustion: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (+ heat); Free radical substitution (with Cl₂ or Br₂ under light)

example.problem: Complete combustion of octane (C₈H₁₈): write the balanced equation and explain why this is the basis of petrol's energy.
example.solution: 2 C₈H₁₈ + 25 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 18 H₂O. Petrol is mostly octane and similar alkanes. Combustion releases enormous energy (≈46 MJ/kg) because C–C and C–H bonds are relatively weak compared to C=O bonds in CO₂; the energy difference fuels our engines.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes are stable, nonreactive hydrocarbons found in crude oil. When you burn them, they release huge amounts of energy.

image.alt: Alkanes: The Saturated Series — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Combustion Reactions: Energy Release
slides.storyContext: Arun watches a demo: Ms. Verma lights ethane gas. A bright blue flame produces heat and light. 'Every hydrocarbon combusts this way,' she explains. 'Complete combustion to CO₂ and H₂O releases the maximum energy.'

example.problem: Balance the combustion of methane (CH₄) and calculate the energy change using bond energies.
example.solution: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413, O=O = 495, C=O = 799, O–H = 467. Bonds broken: 4(413) + 2(495) = 2642 kJ. Bonds formed: 2(799) + 4(467) = 2670 kJ. ΔH ≈ 2642 − 2670 = −28 kJ/mol (actually about −890 kJ/mol per mole of CH₄, showing combustion is highly exothermic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes burn completely in oxygen to produce CO₂ and H₂O, releasing large amounts of heat energy.

image.alt: Combustion Reactions: Energy Release — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkenes: The Unsaturated Players
slides.storyContext: Arun watches a demo: Ms. Verma adds bromine water to a test tube of ethene (C₂H₄). The orange-brown color vanishes instantly. 'The double bond opens up and captures the bromine. Alkenes are busy molecules—always ready to add something. This is why they're so useful in industry.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ (acyclic) or CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (cyclic with one ring)

points.label: Bonding
points.text: One or more C=C (sigma + pi bond); pi bond is the reactive site

points.label: Reactions
points.text: Addition: C=C + H₂, Cl₂, Br₂, H₂O, HCl → add across the double bond

points.label: Markovnikov rule
points.text: When HX (e.g., HCl) adds to an asymmetric alkene, H adds to the C with more H; X adds to the C with fewer H

example.problem: Propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂) reacts with HCl. Which product forms: 1-chloropropane or 2-chloropropane? Explain using Markovnikov's rule.
example.solution: 2-chloropropane (CH₃–CHCl–CH₃). By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the C with more H atoms (the CH₂ end), so Cl adds to the other C. The carbocation at the internal C is more stable (secondary) than at the terminal C (primary), so the reaction favors 2-chloropropane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes have a double bond that's eager to break apart and bond with other atoms. This makes them useful for making plastics and medicines.

image.alt: Alkenes: The Unsaturated Players — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
slides.storyContext: Neha performs a series of tests on ethene (C₂H₄): adding bromine water, adding hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst, adding water in acidic solution.

example.problem: Write the products of these reactions with ethene: (1) + Br₂, (2) + H₂ (Ni catalyst), (3) + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst)
example.solution: (1) C₂H₄ + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane (BrCH₂–CH₂Br, colorless). (2) C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ (ethane). (3) C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (ethanol). All are addition reactions—the double bond opens and new bonds form across it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes undergo addition reactions because the double bond is reactive and can break to form new bonds.

image.alt: Addition Reactions of Alkenes — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkynes: The Triple Bond Specialists
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma holds up a sample of acetylene (C₂H₂). 'This is used in welding torches because it burns at over 3000°C. The triple bond is even more strained and reactive than a double bond. Alkynes are powerful and rare in nature, but chemists use them to build complex molecules.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for terminal alkynes; CₙH₂ₙ₋₄ for internal alkynes

points.label: Bonding
points.text: One C≡C (sigma + two pi bonds); the triple bond is very polarizable

points.label: Reactivity
points.text: Even more reactive than alkenes; can undergo addition, polymerization, and coupling

points.label: Terminal alkyne
points.text: Has an H on the triple-bonded C (—C≡C–H); weakly acidic, can form metal salts

example.problem: Acetylene (HC≡CH) reacts with Br₂. Write the product and explain the step-by-step addition.
example.solution: Step 1: HC≡CH + Br₂ → trans-1,2-dibromoethene (BrCH=CHBr, red color). Step 2: Further addition (if excess Br₂) → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane (BrCH₂–CHBr₂, colorless). Acetylene's triple bond opens in two stages, adding 2 Br at each step.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkynes have a triple bond—the strongest and most reactive C–C linkage. They're rare but incredibly useful in chemistry.

image.alt: Alkynes: The Triple Bond Specialists — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: The Special Ring
slides.storyContext: Neha brings a sample of charred wood from her cooking fire. 'Ms. Verma, I detect a sweet smell. What is it?' Ms. Verma explains: 'Benzene and other aromatics. They come from coal and petroleum. Unlike alkenes, benzene doesn't decolorize bromine easily—its π electrons are delocalized in a resonance-stabilized ring, making it unusually stable. Aromatic compounds are special.'

points.label: Benzene (C₆H₆)
points.text: Hexagonal ring with alternating double bonds (or resonance hybrid with delocalized π electrons)

points.label: Stability
points.text: Resonance delocalization makes benzene extra stable (aromatic); does not undergo addition like alkenes

points.label: Reactions
points.text: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (SEA): an electrophile replaces an H on the ring

points.label: Nitration example
points.text: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ (nitrobenzene); requires a catalyst and heat

example.problem: Explain why benzene (C₆H₆) does NOT decolorize bromine water like alkenes do, even though it has 'double bonds'.
example.solution: Benzene is aromatic: its 6 π electrons are delocalized equally around the ring, creating a resonance-stabilized structure. The 'double bonds' are not true C=C bonds ready to add Br₂. Instead, benzene undergoes substitution (SEA), where an H is replaced, not addition where Br₂ opens a double bond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Benzene and its cousins are 'aromatic'—their rings are so stable and special that they don't react like regular alkenes. They swap atoms rather than add them.

image.alt: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: The Special Ring — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Aromatic Substitution vs. Alkene Addition
slides.storyContext: Arun compares the behavior of benzene and ethene with bromine. Ethene decolorizes bromine water immediately (addition); benzene barely reacts (substitution only occurs with a catalyst).

example.problem: Contrast the reactions of ethene and benzene with Br₂. Why do they react so differently?
example.solution: Ethene (C₂H₄) + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane (BrCH₂–CH₂Br) instantly. The C=C double bond is reactive and adds Br across. Benzene (C₆H₆) + Br₂ → NO REACTION (at room temperature). Requires a catalyst (FeBr₃) and heat for substitution: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr. Benzene's aromatic ring is stabilized by resonance, so it resists disruption and only undergoes substitution, not addition.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes eagerly add bromine; benzene stubbornly refuses—its aromatic ring is just too stable.

image.alt: Aromatic Substitution vs. Alkene Addition — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Worked Example: Predicting Hydrocarbon Reactions
slides.storyContext: Arun is given a mystery hydrocarbon and asks Ms. Verma how to predict its reactions. Ms. Verma walks him through a full analysis: identify the type (alkane, alkene, alkyne, aromatic), predict the reactions, and explain the mechanism.

points.label: Sample: Pent-2-ene (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃)
points.text: Alkene; contains a C=C double bond in the middle chain

points.label: Add H₂ (hydrogenation)
points.text: CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃ + H₂ (catalyst: Ni/Pd) → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (pentane)

points.label: Add Br₂
points.text: Orange bromine is decolorized; product is 2,3-dibromopentane (or the two enantiomers)

points.label: Add HCl
points.text: Markovnikov: Cl adds to the internal C with fewer H, forming 2-chloropentane (secondary carbocation is more stable)

example.problem: Predict the product when pent-2-ene reacts with cold dilute KMnO₄ (oxidation).
example.solution: The double bond in pent-2-ene is cleaved by KMnO₄. Since the C=C is not at the end, products are two ketones: CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ rearranges to give 2-pentanone and some other oxidation products. A purple KMnO₄ solution turns brown (MnO₂) as the oxidation occurs.

slides.inSimpleWords: To predict how a hydrocarbon will react, first identify what type it is. Then apply the rules: alkanes burn or substitute; alkenes and alkynes add; aromatics substitute.

image.alt: Worked Example: Predicting Hydrocarbon Reactions — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Hydrocarbon Reaction Sequence
slides.storyContext: Arun is asked to design a lab procedure to convert ethane (C₂H₆) into ethanol (C₂H₅OH) using only hydrocarbon chemistry. He must plan the steps, predict products, and explain each reaction.

example.problem: Ethane cannot be directly converted to ethanol via addition reactions. Design a route: (a) substitute to form an alkene, (b) use the alkene to introduce oxygen functionality.
example.solution: Step 1: Ethane (C₂H₆) + Br₂ (UV light) → free radical substitution → bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) + HBr. Step 2: Bromoethane + KOH (alcoholic) → elimination → ethene (C₂H₄) + KBr + H₂O. Step 3: Ethene + H₂SO₄ (dilute) + H₂O (hydration) → ethanol (C₂H₅OH). The pathway uses substitution and elimination to form an alkene, then hydration to add the OH group.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons can be converted into each other through a series of well-planned reactions. Identify the starting point, the target, and the pathways in between.

image.alt: Challenge: Design a Hydrocarbon Reaction Sequence — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Classify Unknown Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Neha is given three unknown hydrocarbons and must classify each as alkane, alkene, alkyne, or aromatic based on their reactivity with bromine water and KMnO₄.

example.problem: Sample A: Does NOT decolorize Br₂ water at room temp, requires catalyst and heat. Sample B: Decolorizes Br₂ instantly, orange → colorless. Sample C: Burns to CO₂ and H₂O only, inert to Br₂. Classify each.
example.solution: Sample A: AROMATIC (benzene or derivative). It doesn't add Br₂ without catalyst (stable aromatic ring). Sample B: ALKENE or ALKYNE (most likely alkene). Immediately decolorizes Br₂ via addition. Sample C: ALKANE. Inert to Br₂, only reacts at high temp or with catalysts (substitution).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use bromine water and permanganate tests to distinguish alkanes, alkenes, and aromatic compounds.

image.alt: Challenge: Classify Unknown Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Polymerization: From Alkenes to Plastics
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma holds up a plastic bag. 'This started as ethene from crude oil. Through polymerization, thousands of ethene molecules link together to form polyethylene. This is how we make plastics.'

points.label: Addition polymerization
points.text: Monomers (alkenes) add across their double bonds repeatedly, forming long polymer chains.

points.label: Common polymers
points.text: Polyethylene (from ethene), polypropylene (from propene), polyvinyl chloride / PVC (from vinyl chloride)

points.label: Properties
points.text: Polymers are long-chain hydrocarbons; properties depend on chain length, branching, and cross-linking.

example.problem: Write the polymerization equation for ethene (C₂H₄) to form polyethylene.
example.solution: nC₂H₄ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ (polyethylene). The double bonds in ethene open and link repeatedly, creating a long saturated hydrocarbon chain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes can link together to form long-chain polymers—the basis of plastics used in everything from bags to bottles.

image.alt: Polymerization: From Alkenes to Plastics — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Worked Example: Oil Refining and Fractional Distillation
slides.storyContext: Arun learns about the fractional distillation column at an oil refinery. Crude oil is separated into fractions based on boiling point, which depends on hydrocarbon chain length.

points.label: Fractional distillation
points.text: Crude oil is heated to 350°C, evaporated, and fed into a fractionating column where temperature decreases upward.

points.label: Fractions (top to bottom)
points.text: Petroleum gas (C₁–C₄), petrol (C₅–C₁₀), kerosene (C₁₀–C₁₆), diesel (C₁₆–C₂₀), fuel oil (C₂₀–C₅₀), bitumen (>C₅₀)

points.label: Why it works
points.text: Smaller molecules (lighter hydrocarbons) have lower boiling points and escape as vapor higher up. Larger molecules condense lower down.

example.problem: Why does petrol (C₅–C₁₀) condense in the middle of the fractionating column while bitumen (very long chains) condenses at the bottom?
example.solution: Boiling point increases with chain length (more intermolecular forces). Petrol (smaller) boils at ~170°C, condenses in the warm middle. Bitumen (very large) boils at >350°C, remains liquid until the coolest bottom section.

slides.inSimpleWords: Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by boiling point—longer hydrocarbons boil at higher temps and condense lower in the column.

image.alt: Worked Example: Oil Refining and Fractional Distillation — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Predict Reactivity Based on Structure
slides.storyContext: Neha is given three unknowns—an alkane, an alkene, and an aromatic—and must predict their reactions with Br₂, H₂SO₄, and KMnO₄.

example.problem: Given: (A) hexane (C₆H₁₄), (B) hex-3-ene (C₆H₁₂), (C) benzene (C₆H₆). Predict reactions with Br₂, H₂SO₄, and KMnO₄.
example.solution: Hexane: No reaction with Br₂ (at room temp). No reaction with H₂SO₄ (dilute). Burns to CO₂ + H₂O in KMnO₄ (combustion only). Hex-3-ene: Decolorizes Br₂ (addition). No reaction with dilute H₂SO₄. Oxidized by KMnO₄ (double bond opens). Benzene: No reaction with Br₂ (at room temp, needs FeBr₃ catalyst). No reaction with dilute H₂SO₄. Very resistant to KMnO₄ (aromatic ring is stable).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes are inert; alkenes readily add halogens and are oxidized; aromatics resist addition and oxidation.

slides.title: Sustainability & Alternative Fuels
slides.storyContext: Neha raises an important question: 'Crude oil is a fossil fuel—it will run out. What are we doing to find alternatives?' Ms. Verma explains: 'Biofuels from plants, hydrogen fuel cells, and electric vehicles powered by renewable energy. The chemistry remains hydrocarbon-based or hydrogen-based, but the source is shifting.'

points.text: Biofuels: ethanol from sugarcane, biodiesel from vegetable oil—renewable hydrocarbons
Hydrogen: can be produced from water via electrolysis; burns to H₂O with zero emissions
Electric vehicles: use rechargeable batteries instead of combustion (but storage is key)

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbon chemistry is driving innovation in sustainable fuels and energy storage.

slides.title: Cracking & Reforming: Industrial Hydrocarbon Processing

points.label: Cracking
points.text: Breaking long-chain alkanes into smaller ones by heating with a catalyst. Produces both alkanes and alkenes.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Crude oil refining produces too much heavy fuel oil and not enough petrol. Cracking converts heavy fractions into useful petrol-range hydrocarbons.

points.label: Reforming
points.text: Converting straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes and aromatics to improve octane rating of petrol.

example.problem: What happens when dodecane (C₁₂H₂₆, too large for petrol) is cracked?
example.solution: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ (octane, useful in petrol) + C₄H₈ (butene, useful in polymerization). Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter, more useful products.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cracking and reforming transform crude oil fractions into more valuable products—this is how refineries maximize usable petrol from crude oil.

image.alt: Cracking & Reforming: Industrial Hydrocarbon Processing — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Substitution vs. Addition in Alkanes vs. Alkenes
slides.storyContext: Neha summarizes the key difference between alkane and alkene chemistry: how their C–C bonds determine their reactions.

example.problem: Compare: (1) Ethane + Cl₂ vs. (2) Ethene + Cl₂. Write the products and explain why they're different.
example.solution: (1) C₂H₆ + Cl₂ (UV light, 60°C) → C₂H₅Cl + HCl (SUBSTITUTION: H is replaced by Cl via free-radical mechanism). (2) C₂H₄ + Cl₂ (room temp) → ClCH₂–CH₂Cl (ADDITION: Cl₂ opens the double bond). Different mechanisms and products because ethane has only single bonds (stable); ethene has a reactive π bond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes undergo substitution (swap atoms); alkenes undergo addition (open the double bond). The difference stems from the C–C bond type.

image.alt: Substitution vs. Addition in Alkanes vs. Alkenes — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Structural Isomerism in Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Arun explores how different chain arrangements create isomers with identical formulas but different properties. 'Chain isomers have the same atoms but different boiling points and physical properties.'

points.label: Chain isomers
points.text: Same molecular formula, different carbon chain arrangement (e.g., butane vs. isobutane).

points.label: Position isomers
points.text: Functional group (double bond) at different positions (e.g., pent-1-ene vs. pent-2-ene).

points.label: Property differences
points.text: Isomers have same chemical formula but different bp, density, and reactivity.

example.problem: C₅H₁₀ can be pent-1-ene (CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃) or pent-2-ene (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃). Are they isomers?
example.solution: Yes. Both have C₅H₁₀. They're position isomers—the double bond is at different positions. They have different boiling points and different reactivities (pent-1-ene is terminal, pent-2-ene is internal).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons with the same formula can have different structures—chain isomers and position isomers.

image.alt: Structural Isomerism in Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkyne Reactions: Triple Bond Reactivity
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma demonstrates that alkynes are even more reactive than alkenes. 'The triple bond can add two molecules instead of one. This makes alkynes powerful synthetic intermediates.'

example.problem: Write the products when acetylene (HC≡CH) reacts with (1) H₂ (excess, catalyst) and (2) Br₂ (excess).
example.solution: (1) HC≡CH + 2H₂ (Ni catalyst) → CH₃–CH₃ (ethane, both pi bonds saturated). (2) HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → BrCH₂–CHBr₂ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane, both pi bonds opened and filled with Br).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkynes can add two molecules (or equivalents) because they have two π bonds instead of one.

image.alt: Alkyne Reactions: Triple Bond Reactivity — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons: IUPAC Rules Applied

points.label: Alkane naming
points.text: Identify longest chain, number from nearest end, name substituents: e.g., 2-methylpropane.

points.label: Alkene naming
points.text: Longest chain including C=C, number from end nearest double bond, use suffix -ene: e.g., pent-2-ene.

points.label: Alkyne naming
points.text: Similar to alkenes but with suffix -yne and triple-bond number: e.g., pent-2-yne.

example.problem: Name: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH=CH–CH₃
example.solution: Longest chain: 5 carbons. Double bond present: use -ene. Number from nearest end (C=C at positions 3–4, so number from left: C1-C2-C3=C4-C5). Methyl branch at C2. Name: 2-methylpent-3-ene.

slides.inSimpleWords: IUPAC nomenclature for hydrocarbons follows the same rules: longest chain, functional groups get priority, substituents alphabetically.

image.alt: Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons: IUPAC Rules Applied — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Combustion Analysis of Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Arun learns that burning a hydrocarbon in oxygen tells you its exact composition. 'All the carbon becomes CO₂, all the hydrogen becomes H₂O. By weighing these products, we deduce the C:H ratio.'

example.problem: 0.1 g of a hydrocarbon (unknown CₓHᵧ) burns to give 0.22 g CO₂ and 0.09 g H₂O. Find x and y.
example.solution: Moles of CO₂ = 0.22/44 = 0.005; moles of C = 0.005. Moles of H₂O = 0.09/18 = 0.005; moles of H = 0.01. Ratio C:H = 0.005:0.01 = 1:2. Empirical formula: CH₂. Mass of empirical = 14. Sample mass = 0.1 g, so roughly CH₂ or (CH₂)ₙ for n ≈ 7 if molar mass ≈ 98.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combustion analysis: burn the hydrocarbon, weigh CO₂ and H₂O, deduce C:H ratio.

image.alt: Combustion Analysis of Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Predicting Products: Reaction Type Determines Outcome
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma challenges the class: 'You have an alkane, an alkene, and an aromatic. Given the same reagent (e.g., KMnO₄), each reacts differently or not at all. Predict which reacts and what the product is.'

example.problem: Predict reactions with dilute KMnO₄: (1) butane, (2) but-2-ene, (3) benzene
example.solution: (1) Butane (C₄H₁₀): no reaction (saturated, stable alkane). (2) But-2-ene (C₄H₈): double bond is oxidatively cleaved; purple KMnO₄ turns brown as the C=C is broken. (3) Benzene: very resistant (aromatic); no reaction with dilute KMnO₄ unless heated and concentrated.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbon type determines reactivity: alkanes resist oxidation; alkenes are readily oxidized; aromatics are extremely stable.

slides.title: Recap: Hydrocarbons Power the World
slides.storyContext: As the unit concludes, Arun, Neha, and Ms. Verma reflect on what they've learned. 'Hydrocarbons are everywhere,' Neha says. 'And understanding their structure and reactivity helps us use them wisely—for energy, for materials, and even for the medicines that save lives.'

points.text: Hydrocarbons are compounds of C and H only; classified by C–C bond type
Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂): saturated, stable, react by combustion or substitution
Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ): unsaturated, reactive, undergo addition reactions
Alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂): very reactive, triple bond, used in synthesis and welding
Aromatic hydrocarbons: resonance-stabilized rings, undergo substitution not addition
Reactions follow predictable rules (Markovnikov, free radical, electrophilic substitution)
Hydrocarbons are the foundation of fuels, plastics, medicines, and modern chemistry

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons come in different types—each with its own reactivity and uses. Learn to recognize them, predict their reactions, and harness their power.
